clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder of keratinisation first characterised in Afrikaner families around Oudtshoorn in South Africa
Characterised by cyclical palmoplantar erythema with centrifugal peeling of the stratum corneum, producing annular collarettes of desquamation
Symptoms classically worsen in cold winter weather and improve in summer, hence the name
It is associated with duplications in a regulatory region on chromosome 8 affecting expression of CTSB (cathepsin B)
Affected skin shows recurrent superficial peeling that can extend beyond the palms and soles, sometimes with hyperhidrosis
Diagnosis is clinical, based on the recurrent annular peeling and seasonal pattern with a supportive family history; biopsy shows a distinctive band of parakeratosis with underlying separation
Management is supportive with emollients and keratolytics; some patients benefit from oral retinoids in severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Keratolytic winter erythema is linked to non-coding genomic duplications on chromosome 8 that upregulate cathepsin B, a lysosomal cysteine protease active in keratinocyte differentiation and cornified-envelope turnover. Increased proteolytic activity is thought to promote premature and disordered breakdown of the stratum corneum, so the cornified layer separates and peels in a centrifugal, annular fashion. Environmental cold appears to trigger or accentuate the cycles of erythema and desquamation, explaining the striking seasonal variation.
additionalDifferentials: Palmoplantar exfoliative dermatitis of other cause
Acral peeling from contact or irritant dermatitis
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing a band of parakeratosis with subcorneal or intracorneal separation
Family history and pedigree analysis for autosomal dominant inheritance
Molecular studies of the chromosome 8 regulatory duplication where available
Mycological examination to exclude dermatophyte infection
Patch testing if contact dermatitis is considered
Clinical photography to document the seasonal cyclical pattern
redFlags: Widespread desquamation with barrier failure and secondary infection
Painful fissuring impairing hand or foot function
Atypical persistent lesions not following the seasonal pattern, prompting reconsideration of diagnosis
Signs of secondary bacterial infection in peeling areas
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign, tending to improve after childhood and adolescence, with a chronic relapsing but non-scarring course punctuated by winter exacerbations.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing recurrent peeling as tinea and prescribing repeated antifungals
Overlooking the seasonal history that is central to recognition
Failing to note the autosomal dominant family history
Escalating to systemic therapy before optimising emollient and keratolytic care
management: Emollients and keratolytic agents such as urea or salicylic acid preparations to reduce scaling and peeling
Protection from cold exposure, since winter and cold weather trigger exacerbations
Gentle debridement and topical keratolytics during acute peeling episodes
Management of associated palmoplantar hyperhidrosis where troublesome
Reassurance about the benign, non-scarring course that tends to improve after adolescence
Clinical genetics counselling for this autosomal dominant disorder with family assessment
